```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from statsmodels.tsa.arima.model import ARIMA
from statsmodels.tsa.api import VAR
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

# Bekes & Kezdi's Ch.18 case studies, sourced from their own official data repo
# GitHub raw URLs (once pushed to the student data repo):
# swim_df = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stevenolanecon/7002LBSAI/main/data/swim_tickets.csv")
# cs_df = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stevenolanecon/7002LBSAI/main/data/case_shiller_la.csv")
swim_df = pd.read_csv("data/swim_tickets.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
cs_df = pd.read_csv("data/case_shiller_la.csv", parse_dates=["date"])

# --- Case study A: ABQ swimming pool ticket sales ---
swim_df["month"] = swim_df["date"].dt.month
swim_df["dow"] = swim_df["date"].dt.dayofweek
swim_df["t"] = range(len(swim_df))
swim_train = swim_df[swim_df.date < "2016-01-01"]
swim_test = swim_df[swim_df.date >= "2016-01-01"]

# Seasonality, visually — average tickets by month and by day of week
_month_names = ["Jan","Feb","Mar","Apr","May","Jun","Jul","Aug","Sep","Oct","Nov","Dec"]
_dow_names = ["Mon","Tue","Wed","Thu","Fri","Sat","Sun"]
swim_by_month = [
    {"label": _month_names[m-1], "avg": round(v, 1)}
    for m, v in swim_df.groupby("month")["tickets"].mean().items()
]
swim_by_dow = [
    {"label": _dow_names[d], "avg": round(v, 1)}
    for d, v in swim_df.groupby("dow")["tickets"].mean().items()
]

swim_model_specs = {
    "Trend only": "tickets ~ t",
    "+ month": "tickets ~ t + C(month)",
    "+ month + day of week": "tickets ~ t + C(month) + C(dow)",
}
swim_results = []
_best_pred = None
_best_rmse = np.inf
for name, f in swim_model_specs.items():
    m = smf.ols(f, data=swim_train).fit()
    pred = m.predict(swim_test)
    rmse = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((swim_test["tickets"] - pred) ** 2)))
    swim_results.append({"model": name, "rmse": round(rmse, 1)})
    if rmse < _best_rmse:
        _best_rmse = rmse
        _best_pred = pred

swim_holdout_chart = pd.DataFrame({
    "date": swim_test["date"].dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"),
    "actual": swim_test["tickets"],
    "predicted": _best_pred.round(1),
}).to_dict(orient="records")

# Task reveal — month-only vs trend+month
m_month_only = smf.ols("tickets ~ C(month)", data=swim_train).fit()
rmse_month_only = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((swim_test["tickets"] - m_month_only.predict(swim_test)) ** 2)))
task_swim_output_text = (
    ">>> m_month_only = smf.ols('tickets ~ C(month)', data=train).fit()\n"
    ">>> pred = m_month_only.predict(test)\n"
    ">>> rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean((test['tickets'] - pred) ** 2))\n"
    f">>> round(rmse, 1)\n{round(rmse_month_only, 1)}"
)

# --- Case study B: Case-Shiller LA home price index ---
cs_indexed = cs_df.set_index("date")
cs_indexed.index.freq = "MS"
cs_train = cs_indexed[cs_indexed.index < "2017-01-01"]["price_index_sa"]
cs_test = cs_indexed[(cs_indexed.index >= "2017-01-01") & (cs_indexed.index < "2018-01-01")]["price_index_sa"]

arima_orders = [(1, 1, 0), (2, 1, 0), (1, 1, 1), (2, 0, 0)]
arima_rows = []
_best_arima_fc = None
_best_arima_rmse = np.inf
_best_arima_model = None
for order in arima_orders:
    m = ARIMA(cs_train, order=order).fit()
    fc = m.get_forecast(steps=len(cs_test))
    pred_mean = fc.predicted_mean
    rmse = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((cs_test.values - pred_mean.values) ** 2)))
    arima_rows.append({"order": f"({order[0]},{order[1]},{order[2]})", "rmse": round(rmse, 2), "aic": round(m.aic, 1)})
    if rmse < _best_arima_rmse:
        _best_arima_rmse = rmse
        _best_arima_fc = fc
        _best_arima_model = order

ci = _best_arima_fc.conf_int(alpha=0.2)
arima_forecast_chart = []
_hist = cs_indexed[(cs_indexed.index >= "2015-01-01") & (cs_indexed.index < "2017-01-01")]["price_index_sa"]
for d, v in _hist.items():
    arima_forecast_chart.append({"date": d.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"), "actual": round(float(v), 1), "predicted": None, "lo": None, "hi": None})
for i, d in enumerate(cs_test.index):
    arima_forecast_chart.append({
        "date": d.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"),
        "actual": round(float(cs_test.iloc[i]), 1),
        "predicted": round(float(_best_arima_fc.predicted_mean.iloc[i]), 1),
        "lo": round(float(ci.iloc[i, 0]), 1),
        "hi": round(float(ci.iloc[i, 1]), 1),
    })
best_arima_label = f"ARIMA{_best_arima_model}"
best_arima_rmse_display = round(_best_arima_rmse, 2)

# --- VAR with unemployment ---
cs_var_train = cs_indexed[cs_indexed.index < "2017-01-01"][["price_index_sa", "unemployment_sa"]].diff().dropna()
var_model = VAR(cs_var_train).fit(2)
var_fc = var_model.forecast(cs_var_train.values[-2:], steps=len(cs_test))
_last_level = cs_train.iloc[-1]
var_levels = _last_level + np.cumsum(var_fc[:, 0])
var_rmse = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((cs_test.values - var_levels) ** 2)))
var_rmse_display = round(var_rmse, 2)

ojs_define(
    swim_by_month         = swim_by_month,
    swim_by_dow           = swim_by_dow,
    swim_results          = swim_results,
    swim_holdout_chart    = swim_holdout_chart,
    task_swim_output_text = task_swim_output_text,
    arima_rows            = arima_rows,
    arima_forecast_chart  = arima_forecast_chart,
    best_arima_label      = best_arima_label,
    best_arima_rmse_display = best_arima_rmse_display,
    var_rmse_display      = var_rmse_display,
)
```

## Planning next year's staffing

::: {.instructions-box}
**Business question**: a swimming pool operator needs to know roughly how many tickets will sell each day next year, to plan staffing and opening hours.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Forecasting is a special case of prediction — using only what's happened up to today to say something about tomorrow. Same discipline as Week 10's prediction content, applied to data where "the future" has a very literal meaning.
:::

---

## Forecast horizon and cross-validation

---

## Forecast horizon

- The length of the live time series data still to come — the **forecast horizon**, $H$
- **Short-horizon**: a few periods ahead relative to the data (5 years of monthly data, forecast 3–12 months)
- **Long-horizon**: many periods ahead (5 years of daily data, forecast a year out)

## Why you can't just shuffle and split

Cross-validation with time series is necessary — and genuinely tricky, because a random shuffle destroys the one thing that makes it a time series: order.

::: {.fragment}
Two approaches, matched to the horizon:

- **Insert test sets** — for long-horizon forecasts, where serial correlation and trend matter less. Use all remaining observations, including those after the test set, as training data.
- **Rolling window** — for short-horizon forecasts, where serial correlation matters. Training data always precedes the test set, so nothing "sees the future."
:::

## Insert test sets, visually

```{ojs}
{
  const rows = 4, cols = 20;
  const testStart = [2, 7, 12, 16];
  const rowsHtml = d3.range(rows).map(r => {
    const cells = d3.range(cols).map(c => {
      const inTest = c >= testStart[r] && c < testStart[r] + 3;
      return `<div style="width:22px;height:20px;background:${inTest ? '#5b7fbd' : '#7fbf7f'};border:1px solid white;display:inline-block;"></div>`;
    }).join('');
    return `<div style="margin-bottom:4px;"><span style="display:inline-block;width:60px;font-family:sans-serif;font-size:0.75em;">Set ${r+1}</span>${cells}</div>`;
  }).join('');
  return html`<div>${rowsHtml}<div style="font-family:sans-serif;font-size:0.75em;color:#555;margin-top:8px;">
    <span style="color:#2d6a4f;">■</span> training &nbsp; <span style="color:#5b7fbd;">■</span> test — test sets scattered through the series, training uses everything else
  </div></div>`
}
```

## Rolling window, visually

```{ojs}
{
  const rows = 4, cols = 20;
  const trainEnd = [6, 9, 12, 15];
  const rowsHtml = d3.range(rows).map(r => {
    const cells = d3.range(cols).map(c => {
      let color = "#eee";
      if (c < trainEnd[r]) color = "#2d6a4f";
      else if (c < trainEnd[r] + 3) color = "#5b7fbd";
      return `<div style="width:22px;height:20px;background:${color};border:1px solid white;display:inline-block;"></div>`;
    }).join('');
    return `<div style="margin-bottom:4px;"><span style="display:inline-block;width:60px;font-family:sans-serif;font-size:0.75em;">Set ${r+1}</span>${cells}</div>`;
  }).join('');
  return html`<div>${rowsHtml}<div style="font-family:sans-serif;font-size:0.75em;color:#555;margin-top:8px;">
    <span style="color:#2d6a4f;">■</span> training &nbsp; <span style="color:#5b7fbd;">■</span> test — training always precedes test, the window rolls forward
  </div></div>`
}
```

## Long-horizon: trend and seasonality

---

## Two ways to model a trend

- **Average change**: $\hat y_{T+H} = y_T + H \times \widehat{\Delta y}$ — carries forward from the last observation
- **Trend line**: $\hat y_t = \hat\alpha + \hat\delta t$ — assumes $y$ stays close to a fitted line, so one unusual last observation matters less
- Neither is inherently better — depends whether you trust the series to keep going from where it is, or to revert to its long-run pattern

## Case study: swimming pool ticket sales

- Daily ticket sales, Albuquerque, 2010–2016 — big data, real transactions
- Business question already on the table: forecast next year's daily demand
- Clear seasonality: summer months and weekends dominate

```{ojs}
{
  const monthChart = Plot.plot({
    width: 340, height: 410,
    x: {label: "Month", domain: swim_by_month.map(d => d.label)},

    marks: [Plot.barY(swim_by_month, {x: "label", y: "avg", fill: "#5b7fbd"}), Plot.ruleY([0])]
  })
  const dowChart = Plot.plot({

    x: {label: "Day of week", domain: swim_by_dow.map(d => d.label)},
    y: {label: "Avg. tickets/day"},

  })

}
```

## Building up the model, on real data

```{.python}
model_specs = {
    "Trend only": "tickets ~ t",
    "+ month": "tickets ~ t + C(month)",
    "+ month + day of week": "tickets ~ t + C(month) + C(dow)",
}

results = []
for name, formula in model_specs.items():
    model = smf.ols(formula, data=train).fit()
    pred = model.predict(test)
    rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean((test["tickets"] - pred) ** 2))
    results.append({"model": name, "rmse": round(rmse, 1)})
```

```{ojs}
{

}
```

Trained on 2010–2015, tested on 2016 — a genuine holdout the model never saw. Seasonality does almost all of the work; the linear trend barely matters on its own.

## Short-horizon: AR and ARIMA

---

## Autoregressive models

$$y_t^E = \beta_0 + \beta_1 y_{t-1}$$

- The simplest **AR(1)** model: today's value predicted from yesterday's alone
- $\beta_1$ is just the first-order serial correlation coefficient from the workshop, wearing a forecasting hat
- $\beta_1 = 1$ is a random walk; $\beta_1 = 0$ is white noise — nothing left to forecast from the series itself

## The innovation

$$e_t = y_t - y_t^E \qquad y_t = y_t^E + e_t$$

The **innovation**: what's genuinely new in $y_t$, on top of everything predictable from its own past. Formally the same idea as a prediction error — but now it's *past* innovations doing the predicting.

## ARIMA, built from three letters

- **AR(p)**: predict $y_t$ from up to $p$ of its own lags
- **I(d)**: whether the model is written in $y$ itself ($d=0$) or its $d$-th difference
- **MA(q)**: a linear combination of past innovations, $y_t = e_t + \theta_1 e_{t-1} + \dots + \theta_q e_{t-q}$ — captures serial correlation that drops to zero sharply after a few lags, a different pattern than AR
- **ARIMA(p,d,q)** combines all three, flexible enough to approximate almost any serial correlation pattern

## Case study: Case-Shiller home price index

- Monthly home price index, Los Angeles, 2000–2018 (FRED)
- Train on 2000–2016, forecast 12 months into 2017 — a genuine holdout
- Try a few $(p,d,q)$ specifications, pick by holdout RMSE — exactly the model-selection discipline from Week 10

```{.python}
from statsmodels.tsa.arima.model import ARIMA

model = ARIMA(train, order=(2, 1, 0)).fit()
forecast = model.get_forecast(steps=12)
```

::: {.fragment}
$(2,0,0)$ — no differencing, fitted on the level of the index — is clearly the worst. The undifferenced series isn't stationary, and the forecast pays for it.
:::

## VAR — bringing in other variables

---

## Forecasting with help from x

- Short-horizon forecasts often improve with other variables — but now you need **forecasts of those too**
- **Vector autoregression (VAR)**: a set of time series regressions, one per variable, where every equation's right-hand side is lags of every variable in the system

$$y_t^E = \beta_{10} + \beta_{11}y_{t-1} + \beta_{12}x_{t-1} \qquad x_t^E = \beta_{20} + \beta_{21}y_{t-1} + \beta_{22}x_{t-1}$$

- More coefficients to estimate means more estimation error — the hope is that $x$ still nets out an improvement

## Does it help here?

Adding California's unemployment rate to a VAR(2), forecasting the same 2017 holdout:

```{.python}
from statsmodels.tsa.api import VAR

# Both series first-differenced — VAR needs stationary inputs, same logic as Section C
var_train = df[["price_index_sa", "unemployment_sa"]].diff().dropna()

var_model = VAR(var_train).fit(2)
var_forecast_diffs = var_model.forecast(var_train.values[-2:], steps=len(test))

# Undo the differencing: cumulative sum of forecast differences, added back onto
# the last known level
var_levels = train.iloc[-1] + np.cumsum(var_forecast_diffs[:, 0])
var_rmse = np.sqrt(np.mean((test.values - var_levels) ** 2))
```

```{ojs}
{
  return html`<div style="text-align:center;padding-top:10px;">
    <table style="margin:0 auto;font-family:sans-serif;font-size:1.1em;border-collapse:collapse;">
      <tr style="border-bottom:2px solid #1a1a2e;"><th style="padding:6px 26px;">Model</th><th style="padding:6px 26px;">Holdout RMSE</th></tr>
      <tr style="border-bottom:1px solid #ddd;"><td style="padding:5px 26px;">Best ARIMA (<code>${best_arima_label}</code>)</td><td style="padding:5px 26px;text-align:center;">${best_arima_rmse_display}</td></tr>
      <tr><td style="padding:5px 26px;">VAR(2) with unemployment</td><td style="padding:5px 26px;text-align:center;font-weight:700;">${var_rmse_display}</td></tr>
    </table>
  </div>`
}
```

::: {.fragment}
Here, VAR genuinely improves on the best ARIMA — unemployment carries real information about where home prices are heading. Not guaranteed in general: Gabor & Kézdi's own version of this case study found VAR *didn't* help on their sample window. Same method, different window, different answer — a real lesson about external validity on its own.
:::

---

## External validity in time series

---

## The one assumption everything rests on

- External validity in forecasting means **stationarity**: the patterns you learned from the training data — trend, seasonality, correlation structure — have to still hold in the live data
- This is a much bigger risk in time series than in cross-sectional prediction, because forecasting is *by design* about a period you've never observed
- No amount of cross-validation on historical data can fully rule this out — a genuine structural break (a pandemic, a housing crash) breaks every model here equally

## Summary

- Forecasting is prediction with a time index — but cross-validation has to respect order: inserted test sets for long horizons, rolling windows for short ones
- Long-horizon forecasts lean on trend and seasonality — often seasonality alone does most of the work
- Short-horizon forecasts lean on serial correlation — AR and ARIMA models capture it directly, chosen by holdout RMSE like any other prediction model
- VAR can improve a forecast by bringing in other variables, at the cost of needing to forecast those too — and whether it actually helps is itself an empirical, not automatic, question
